passages.text: Chromosome 22q13 terminal deletion size is associated with relevant clinical features in a sample of 63 Italian patients with Phelan-McDermid syndrome
Background

Phelan-McDermid syndrome (PMS) is caused in the majority of cases by the loss or mutation of one allele of the <italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic> gene, located in human chr 22q13.33. <sentence_start/>PMS displays large interindividual differences in clinical severity and longitudinal trajectory. <sentence_start/>Other genes located in this chromosomal region are known to contribute to the clinical phenotype (<italic toggle="yes">CELSR1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">TCF20</italic>) in patients with larger deletions. <sentence_start/>The aim of this study is to identify clinically-relevant phenotypic features significantly influenced by the size of chromosome 22q terminal deletion and to identify new potential candidate genes likely to be involved in these phenotypic effects.
Methods

Genotype-phenotype correlations were investigated in 63 PMS patients directly ascertained by deep clinical phenotyping and determination of deletion size (Agilent CGH-array 180K or 400K). <sentence_start/>Patients were partitioned into eleven categories, based on deletion size (Mb). <sentence_start/>Phenotypic variables significantly influenced by deletion size were initially detected by exact χ<sup>2</sup> (10,000 iterations) and Kendall’s Tau. <sentence_start/>Candidate genes were then sought using: (a) ROC curves for binary dichotomous variables; (b) best separation threshold for quantitative variables.
Results

Phenotypic variables significantly associated with chromosome 22q deletion size in our sample include: expressive language (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> < 0.001); motor development timing (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> < 0.001); gait (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> < 0.001); muscle strength (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> < 0.01); social cognition, encompassing eye contact, exchange gesture, and joint attention (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> < 0.001-< 0.05); infectious diseases coincident with the onset of behavioral manifestations (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> < 0.001); brain structural abnormalities on MRI (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> < 0.001); dysmorphisms (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> < 0.001); renal and urinary malformations (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> < 0.01); comorbid lifelong bipolar disorder (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> < 0.05). <sentence_start/>The best separation thresholds for many of these variables were located within or nearby genes playing important morphogenetic (<italic toggle="yes">PLXNB2, TAFA5</italic>) or neurodevelopmental roles (<italic toggle="yes">BRD1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">TBC1D22A</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">ATXN10</italic> and/or <italic toggle="yes">FBLN1</italic>). <sentence_start/>For renal malformations, the two best thresholds point toward one long non-coding RNA and a cluster of antisense RNAs.
Conclusions

The genes identified in this study appear as strong candidates to contribute to the PMS phenotype, by conferring an additional layer of abnormal neurodevelopment and impaired morphogenesis to the disruptive effects produced by <italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic> haploinsufficiency.

Introduction

Phelan-McDermid syndrome (PMS), also known as “chromosome 22q13.3 deletion syndrome” (OMIM #606,232), is a rare genetic disorder mainly characterized by global developmental delay and/or intellectual disability, muscle hypotonia, severely impaired or absent speech, and minor/major dysmorphisms [<citation rid="CR1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/1096-8628(20010615)101:2<91::aid-ajmg1340>3.0.co;2-c" pmid="11391650" count="1">1</citation>-<citation rid="CR3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/2040-2392-4-18" pmid="23758760" pmcid="PMC3707861" count="1">3</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Patients may also present several medical conditions, including abnormal EEG (with or without seizures) [<citation rid="CR4" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13229-018-0205-9" pmid="29719671" pmcid="PMC5921983" count="1">4</citation>-<citation rid="CR6" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.seizure.2014.06.008" pmid="25027555" count="1">6</citation>], structural brain anomalies at the MRI [<citation rid="CR7" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ajmg.a.33253" pmcid="PMC3119894" pmid="20186804" count="1">7</citation>-<citation rid="CR10" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ajmg.a.35700" pmcid="PMC3733662" pmid="23225497" count="1">10</citation>], sleep disturbances [<citation rid="CR11" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/sleep/zsw062" pmid="28364490" count="1">11</citation>, <citation rid="CR12" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.7554/eLife.42819" pmid="30973326" pmcid="PMC6488297" count="1">12</citation>], renal malformations, gastroesophageal reflux, lymphedema [<citation rid="CR13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/cge.14364" pmid="37232218" count="1">13</citation>-<citation rid="CR15" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ejmg.2023.104754" pmid="37003575" count="1">15</citation>], and immune deficits [<citation rid="CR3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/2040-2392-4-18" pmid="23758760" pmcid="PMC3707861" count="1">3</citation>, <citation rid="CR14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s11689-019-9273-1" pmcid="PMC6637483" pmid="31319798" count="1">14</citation>, <citation rid="CR16" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00439-014-1423-7" pmid="24481935" count="1">16</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The exact prevalence of PMS is still unknown. <sentence_start/>Currently, over 3,600 PMS individuals worldwide are registered in the PMS Foundation Registry [<citation rid="CR17" ref-type="bibr" count="1">17</citation>]; however, the syndrome is likely underdiagnosed, given its nonspecific clinical phenotype and the need for genetic testing [<citation rid="CR18" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/2040-2392-4-17" pmid="23758743" pmcid="PMC3695795" count="1">18</citation>, <citation rid="CR19" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/jmedgenet-2011-100225" pmid="21984749" count="1">19</citation>].

The most frequent cause of PMS is represented by terminal deletions of chromosome 22q13.3 involving the <italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic> gene, in a minority of cases due to ring chromosome 22 or to unbalanced translocations, followed by <italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic> intragenic deletions and pathogenic mutations [<citation rid="CR1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/1096-8628(20010615)101:2<91::aid-ajmg1340>3.0.co;2-c" pmid="11391650" count="1">1</citation>, <citation rid="CR2" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1159/000334260" pmid="22670140" pmcid="PMC3366702" count="1">2</citation>, <citation rid="CR4" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13229-018-0205-9" pmid="29719671" pmcid="PMC5921983" count="1">4</citation>, <citation rid="CR20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/jmg.40.8.575" pmid="12920066" pmcid="PMC1735560" count="1">20</citation>]. <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic> encodes for a scaffolding protein abounding in the postsynaptic density (PSD) of glutamatergic synapses and is involved in dendritic spines and synapse formation [<citation rid="CR21" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1074/jbc.M111.258384" pmid="21795692" pmcid="PMC3186429" count="1">21</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Within the framework of PMS, in addition to global developmental delay and intellectual disability, <italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic> haploinsufficiency promotes other frequently co-occurring behavioral conditions, like bipolar disorder [<citation rid="CR22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2147/NDT.S30506" pmid="22570549" pmcid="PMC3346055" count="1">22</citation>-<citation rid="CR25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s11689-020-9309-6" pmid="32050889" pmcid="PMC7014655" count="1">25</citation>], catatonia [<citation rid="CR24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13229-019-0291-3" pmid="31879555" pmcid="PMC6930682" count="1">24</citation>-<citation rid="CR27" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1017/S0033291725100536" pmid="40509778" pmcid="PMC12180507" count="1">27</citation>], and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) [<citation rid="CR28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ajmg.b.32528" pmid="28371232" count="1">28</citation>-<citation rid="CR33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ajmg.b.30822" pmid="18615476" count="1">33</citation>], with a diagnosis of ASD sometimes preceding the results of genetic testing by several years in clinical practice. <sentence_start/>Also <italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic> mutations represent one of the most common monogenic cause of autism, especially in cases with moderate to profound intellectual disability [<citation rid="CR31" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.braindev.2012.05.013" pmid="22749736" count="1">31</citation>, <citation rid="CR34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1086/522590" pmid="17999366" pmcid="PMC2276348" count="1">34</citation>, <citation rid="CR35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13023-020-01592-5" pmid="33256793" pmcid="PMC7708101" count="1">35</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The latter observation, coupled with the fact that usually even the smallest pathogenic deletions at least partly span <italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic> [<citation rid="CR7" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ajmg.a.33253" pmcid="PMC3119894" pmid="20186804" count="1">7</citation>, <citation rid="CR14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s11689-019-9273-1" pmcid="PMC6637483" pmid="31319798" count="1">14</citation>, <citation rid="CR19" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/jmedgenet-2011-100225" pmid="21984749" count="1">19</citation>], has long proven its pathogenic role in the PMS phenotype [<citation rid="CR9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1086/321293" pmid="11431708" pmcid="PMC1235301" count="1">9</citation>, <citation rid="CR20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/jmg.40.8.575" pmid="12920066" pmcid="PMC1735560" count="1">20</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, interstitial chromosome 22q deletions sparing <italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic> have also been found associated with PMS, albeit occasionally [<citation rid="CR16" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00439-014-1423-7" pmid="24481935" count="1">16</citation>, <citation rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ajmg.a.36513" pmid="24700646" count="1">36</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This rare but important finding further underscores the phenotypic roles of additional genes centromeric to <italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic> in the chromosome 22q region, and has led to propose a distinction between “<italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic>-related” and “<italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic>-unrelated” PMS [<citation rid="CR37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13023-022-02180-5" pmid="35093143" pmcid="PMC8800328" count="1">37</citation>].

Great interindividual heterogeneity can be clinically observed among PMS patients. <sentence_start/>This heterogeneity may at least partly be explained by phenotypic contributions by 22q13 genes other than <italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic> [<citation rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ajmg.a.36513" pmid="24700646" count="1">36</citation>-<citation rid="CR39" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ajmg.a.62222" pmid="33949759" pmcid="PMC8251815" count="1">39</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Deletion size can vary from less than 100 kb to > 9 Mb in PMS [<citation rid="CR16" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00439-014-1423-7" pmid="24481935" count="1">16</citation>, <citation rid="CR40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13229-024-00619-z" pmid="39350236" pmcid="PMC11443936" count="1">40</citation>], and genotype-phenotype studies indicate that larger deletions generally lead to more severe symptomatology [<citation rid="CR41" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0253859" pmid="34228749" pmcid="PMC8259982" count="1">41</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Larger deletions have been associated with severity of developmental delay, including absent or impaired speech and walking ability [<citation rid="CR16" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00439-014-1423-7" pmid="24481935" count="1">16</citation>, <citation rid="CR19" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/jmedgenet-2011-100225" pmid="21984749" count="1">19</citation>, <citation rid="CR40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13229-024-00619-z" pmid="39350236" pmcid="PMC11443936" count="1">40</citation>, <citation rid="CR42" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s11689-021-09370-5" pmid="34246244" pmcid="PMC8272382" count="1">42</citation>, <citation rid="CR43" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/gim.2013.144" pmid="24136618" count="1">43</citation>]; abnormal growth, including macrocephaly and large hands [<citation rid="CR16" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00439-014-1423-7" pmid="24481935" count="1">16</citation>, <citation rid="CR42" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s11689-021-09370-5" pmid="34246244" pmcid="PMC8272382" count="1">42</citation>]; neonatal hypotonia [<citation rid="CR40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13229-024-00619-z" pmid="39350236" pmcid="PMC11443936" count="1">40</citation>, <citation rid="CR43" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/gim.2013.144" pmid="24136618" count="1">43</citation>]; dysmorphic features [<citation rid="CR3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/2040-2392-4-18" pmid="23758760" pmcid="PMC3707861" count="1">3</citation>, <citation rid="CR16" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00439-014-1423-7" pmid="24481935" count="1">16</citation>, <citation rid="CR40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13229-024-00619-z" pmid="39350236" pmcid="PMC11443936" count="1">40</citation>]; number of medical comorbidities [<citation rid="CR3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/2040-2392-4-18" pmid="23758760" pmcid="PMC3707861" count="1">3</citation>]; seizures [<citation rid="CR40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13229-024-00619-z" pmid="39350236" pmcid="PMC11443936" count="1">40</citation>]; adaptive skills [<citation rid="CR44" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s11689-016-9150-0" pmid="27118998" pmcid="PMC4845478" count="1">44</citation>]; renal abnormalities and lymphedema [<citation rid="CR14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s11689-019-9273-1" pmcid="PMC6637483" pmid="31319798" count="1">14</citation>, <citation rid="CR40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13229-024-00619-z" pmid="39350236" pmcid="PMC11443936" count="1">40</citation>]; congenital heart defects, neuroimaging brain anomalies and recurrent infections [<citation rid="CR40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13229-024-00619-z" pmid="39350236" pmcid="PMC11443936" count="1">40</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Some studies have attempted to precisely identify chromosome 22q13 genomic regions or candidate genes responsible for specific clinical features in PMS. <sentence_start/>For instance, Sarasua and Colleagues [<citation rid="CR43" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/gim.2013.144" pmid="24136618" count="1">43</citation>] identified genomic regions significantly associated with absent speech (boundaries: 40.4-49.4 Mb, median deletion size: 7.0 Mb), delayed speech (boundaries: 44.4-49.5, median deletion size: 3.3 Mb), macrocephaly, tall stature, and large or flashy hands (boundaries 44.5-46.6 Mb). <sentence_start/>Interestingly, the genomic region spanning 41.9 to 46.6 Mb was associated with decreased prevalence of autism and aggressive behavior [<citation rid="CR43" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/gim.2013.144" pmid="24136618" count="1">43</citation>]. <sentence_start/>To date the gene with the best established role in PMS besides <italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic> is <italic toggle="yes">TCF20</italic>, responsible for an autosomal dominant form of intellectual disability, with developmental delay, muscle hypotonia, variable dysmorphic features, movement disorders, and sleep disturbances [<citation rid="CR45" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13073-019-0623-0" pmid="30819258" pmcid="PMC6393995" count="1">45</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This gene, however, is included only in the largest terminal deletions found in a small minority of PMS patients (see Results). <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">CELSR1</italic> is another gene located on chromosome 22q13 whose haploinsufficiency has been demonstrated significantly associated with the risk to develop lymphedema in PMS [<citation rid="CR13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/cge.14364" pmid="37232218" count="1">13</citation>].

The purpose of the present study is to move beyond the well-established role of <italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic> in PMS and to investigate the contributions provided by other genes to a set of clinically relevant phenotypic features in a sample of 63 directly-ascertained Italian PMS patients carrying 22q13 deletions of various sizes. <sentence_start/>Understanding the impact of deletion size and related genes on the clinical phenotype and on the developmental trajectory of PMS patients is important, because it can foster more reliable predictions, personalized diagnostics, and evidence-based management strategies.
Methods
Participants

Seventy children, adolescents, and adults with a genetic diagnosis of Phelan-McDermid syndrome were recruited at the Campus Bio-Medico University Hospital (Rome, Italy), and at the Interdepartmental Program “Autism 0-90” of the “G. Martino” University Hospital of Messina (Italy), where they were referred for medical follow-up and treatment. <sentence_start/>This sample underwent deep phenotyping and its clinical, demographic, and developmental characteristics have been recently described [<citation rid="CR46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s11689-024-09572-7" pmid="39363263" pmcid="PMC11451156" count="1">46</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Five patients were excluded, because they carried a disruptive <italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic> point mutations, and two because they lacked exact deletion size determination by array-based technologies, although the presence of a deletion had been demonstrated by FISH. <sentence_start/>Ultimately, sixty-three patients were included in the present study, 31 females and 32 males, with mean (±S.D.) age 12.2 ± 10.1 years (range 1.7-44.0 years). <sentence_start/>Their demographic and genetic characteristics, intellectual level, and clinical DMS-5 diagnoses are summarized in Table 1. <sentence_start/>A formal DSM-5 diagnosis of ASD was given to 25.4% of cases, yielding an ASD prevalence that is lower than that reported in other studies [<citation rid="CR3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/2040-2392-4-18" pmid="23758760" pmcid="PMC3707861" count="1">3</citation>, <citation rid="CR47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13023-015-0323-9" pmid="26306707" pmcid="PMC4549933" count="1">47</citation>, <citation rid="CR48" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/hmg/ddab280" pmcid="PMC8863417" pmid="34559195" count="1">48</citation>] (see Discussion).

This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of University ‘‘Campus Bio-Medico’’ of Rome, Italy (protocol n. 14/98, first approval on April 28, 1998 and subsequent amendments) and by the Ethics Committee of Messina, Italy (protocol n. 22/17, approved on June 19, 2017). <sentence_start/>All parents gave written informed consent for themselves and for their affected offspring. <sentence_start/>All procedures performed in studies involving human participants are in accordance with the ethical standards of the institutional and/or national research committee and with the Helsinki declaration (2000).
Assessment and outcome measures

All patients underwent an in-depth clinical assessment, as described [<citation rid="CR46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s11689-024-09572-7" pmid="39363263" pmcid="PMC11451156" count="1">46</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Briefly, patient and family history were collected, and a thorough medical, neurological and neuropsychological evaluation was performed. <sentence_start/>Standardized instruments administered included Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule - 2 (ADOS-2) [<citation rid="CR49" ref-type="bibr" count="1">49</citation>] and Autism Diagnostic Interview - Revised (ADI-R) [<citation rid="CR50" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/BF02172145" pmid="7814313" count="1">50</citation>] for the evaluation of autistic symptomatology; the Repetitive Behavior Scale - Revised (RBS-R) [<citation rid="CR51" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10803-006-0213-z" pmid="17048092" count="1">51</citation>] and the Short Sensory Profile (SSP) [<citation rid="CR52" ref-type="bibr" count="1">52</citation>] for the evaluation of repetitive behaviors and sensory processing patterns, respectively; the Aberrant Behavior Checklist (ABC) [<citation rid="CR53" ref-type="bibr" pmid="3993694" count="1">53</citation>] and the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL) [<citation rid="CR54" ref-type="bibr" count="1">54</citation>] to assess problematic behaviors; the Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scale-II (VABS-II), [<citation rid="CR55" ref-type="bibr" count="1">55</citation>] to assess adaptive behaviors. <sentence_start/>Intellectual/developmental quotient was evaluated with the Griffiths Scales of Child Development- III [<citation rid="CR56" ref-type="bibr" count="1">56</citation>], Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children-Fourth Edition (WISC-IV) [<citation rid="CR57" ref-type="bibr" count="1">57</citation>], or the Leiter-3 scale [<citation rid="CR58" ref-type="bibr" count="1">58</citation>], depending on age and language skills. <sentence_start/>Finally, the Quality of Life in Autism Questionnaire (QOL-A) [<citation rid="CR59" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10803-017-3402-z" pmid="29188584" pmcid="PMC5889785" count="1">59</citation>] and the World Health Organization's Quality of Life Questionnaire (WHOQOL) [<citation rid="CR60" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1017/s0033291798006667" pmid="9626712" count="1">60</citation>] were administered separately to mothers and fathers to assess parental quality of life.
Genetic analysis

To determine deletion size, all 63 patients underwent CGH-array (Agilent 180 K or 400 K), as described in our previous studies [<citation rid="CR61" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mgg3.1939" pmid="35762097" pmcid="PMC9356560" count="1">61</citation>, <citation rid="CR62" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mgg3.2182" pmid="37186221" pmcid="PMC10422062" count="1">62</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Karyotype analysis was performed to investigate the presence of a ring chromosome 22, which was detected in 6/63 (9.5%) deleted PMS patients (Table 1). <sentence_start/>The detection of postzygotic mosaic deletions by CGH-array displays variable sensitivity depending on array technology and deleted chromosomal region [<citation rid="CR63" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/1755-8166-3-11" pmid="20587050" pmcid="PMC2909945" count="1">63</citation>, <citation rid="CR64" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/1755-8166-4-13" pmid="21554683" pmcid="PMC3101650" count="1">64</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In order to enhance reliability, we applied a minimum 30% mosaicism threshold [<citation rid="CR63" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/1755-8166-3-11" pmid="20587050" pmcid="PMC2909945" count="1">63</citation>], which identified 4/63 (6.5%) cases carrying postmitotic mosaic deletions (Table 1). <sentence_start/>All genomic coordinates correspond to the 2009 human genome build 19 (GRCh37/NCBI build 37.1). <sentence_start/>Deletion coordinates were plotted using the University of California at Santa Cruz Genome Browser ( ). <sentence_start/>The length of all deletions is expressed as distance in kb from the telomere, identified as the hg19 genomic coordinate Chr22:51,244,566 (chr22_jh806586_fix).
Genotype-phenotype correlations

Participants were distributed into eleven categories, according to deletion size (Fig. 1). <sentence_start/>The eleven categories were defined, as follows: patients carrying the smallest telomeric deletions, spanning only <italic toggle="yes">SHANK3, ACR,</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">RABL2B</italic>, fell into category n. 1 (< 132 kb in size, derived from nt 51,244,566-51,112,836/hg19). <sentence_start/>The remaining 10 categories include patients carrying increasingly larger deletions, with proximal breakpoint moving toward the centromere by 1 Mb per category, up to category 11, which includes the largest deletion found in our sample (9.008 Mb) (Fig. 1). <sentence_start/>Table 2 lists the most functionally relevant genes spanned by each chromosomal segment, as well as the number and percentages of participants carrying deletions which fall into each category. <sentence_start/>In simple terms, patients included in each category carry deletions spanning at least some telomeric genes present in that segment, plus all genes listed in the preceding categories (see Fig. 1 for graphical representation). <sentence_start/>Phenotypic variables significantly correlated with deletion size were not sought based on an a-priori hypothesis, but rather using an unbiased approach starting from 48 behavioral, medical, neurological, and patient history variables from our data set [<citation rid="CR46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s11689-024-09572-7" pmid="39363263" pmcid="PMC11451156" count="1">46</citation>], after excluding results from tests and questionnaires. <sentence_start/>We first performed Kendall’s tau and an association χ<sup>2</sup> test with the Monte Carlo procedure (10,000 iterations). <sentence_start/>Phenotypic variables reaching at least nominal significance with both tests were then further analyzed using two different statistical methods, in order to identify the associated candidate region, the maximum likelihood threshold, and the best candidate genes possibly responsible for each phenotype. <sentence_start/>For binary dichotomous phenotypic variables, the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) method [<citation rid="CR65" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/JTO.0b013e3181ec173d" pmid="20736804" count="1">65</citation>] was used to evaluate all possible genomic breakpoint positions above which a given phenotype becomes aberrant. <sentence_start/>The maximum likelihood threshold was determined according to the Youden’s index (J = sensitivity + specificity-1), while the area under the curve (AUC) was calculated to determine whether the threshold identified was significantly capable to distinguish between “normal” and “abnormal” phenotype. <sentence_start/>The second method defined the best separation threshold as the optimal binary division that results in maximum heterogeneity between groups and homogeneity within groups. <sentence_start/>This method is similar to that of recursive partitioning, and the goodness of the division was measured by the complexity parameter (CP). <sentence_start/>For quantitative variables, the CP is equal to the proportion of variance explained by the binary partition, while for categorial variables it is proportional to the reduction of the generalized Gini impurity index. <sentence_start/>Statistical significance was set at <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> < 0.05, Prediction of the functional impact of haploinsufficiency for candidate genes

The functional impact of haploinsufficiency for the most promising candidates genes potentially involved in each phenotype was assessed using the “probability of being loss-of-function intolerant” (pLI) [<citation rid="CR67" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nature19057" pmid="27535533" pmcid="PMC5018207" count="1">67</citation>], the “Loss-of-function Observed/Expected Upper-bound Fraction” (LOEUF) score [<citation rid="CR68" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-020-2308-7" pmid="32461654" pmcid="PMC7334197" count="1">68</citation>], and the “probability of haploinsufficiency” score (pHaplo) [<citation rid="CR69" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2022.06.036" pmid="35917817" pmcid="PMC9742861" count="1">69</citation>]. <sentence_start/>pLI and LOEUF were derived from gnomAD v4.1.0, pHaplo from UCSC Genome Browser hg38. <sentence_start/>In addition, transcriptional sensitivity to haploinsufficiency was empirically derived from the blood transcriptomic study by Breen et al., [<citation rid="CR70" ref-type="bibr" pmid="36276299" doi="10.1016/j.xhgg.2022.100145" pmcid="PMC9579712" count="1">70</citation>], who contrasted PMS patients with large vs small deletions.
Results

Among the 63 patients included in this study, 55 (87.3%) carry simple terminal deletions of chromosome 22q13, six (9.5%) have a deletion in the context of a ring chromosome 22, and 2 carry unbalanced translocations (Table 1). <sentence_start/>Deletion size varied from 25 kb to 9.008 Mb (median: 1.847 kb) [<citation rid="CR46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s11689-024-09572-7" pmid="39363263" pmcid="PMC11451156" count="1">46</citation>].
Phenotypic variables associated with deletion size

Fourteen phenotypic variables, including some well-known PMS characteristics and several clinically relevant non-specific features, displayed a significant association with deletion size applying <italic toggle="yes">both</italic> Kendall’s tau and an association χ<sup>2</sup> test with Monte Carlo exact p-value estimation (Table 3). <sentence_start/>For the majority of these variables, both nominal <italic toggle="yes">p</italic>-values were < 0.001 (< 0.05 after Bonferroni’s correction). <sentence_start/>The fourteen variables associated with deletion size and listed in Table 3 fall into five domains:
language development:
presence/absence of verbal language;
level of verbal language (no verbal language/words only/words and sentences);
first sentences acquisition timing.
motor function and development:
timing of motor development (typical/delayed/not walking);
gait (normal/abnormal/not walking);
muscle strength (normal/reduced).
social cognition;
eye contact (normal/inconsistent/absent);
exchange gesture (complete/incomplete/absent);
joint attention (complete/incomplete/absent).
medical issues:
structural abnormalities on brain MRI;
presence/absence of an infectious disease at the onset of behavioral symptoms;
renal abnormalities and malformations:
dysmorphisms.
comorbid disorders;
lifetime diagnosis of bipolar disorder (present/absent).
Genotype-phenotype correlation: identification of candidate genes

ROC curve analysis and the optimal separation method led to the identification of one to three “best cut-offs” or “ROC curve peaks” along chromosome 22q13 for each variable (Table 3): for uniformity, these peaks will hereby be defined “maximum likelihood thresholds”. <sentence_start/>In simple terms, the transition from normal to altered phenotype provides relevant information on candidate genes that, if haploinsufficient, significantly enhance the probability of appearance of the phenotype under scrutiny.

Maximum likelihood thresholds are displayed in Fig. 2. <sentence_start/>Patient counts by deletion size category are presented in Tables 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, where the transition from normal to altered phenotype is emphasized in bold and thick lines highlight the boundary closest to each maximum likelihood threshold (i.e., best cut-offs or ROC curve peaks, as listed in Table 3 and displayed in Fig. 2). <sentence_start/>Detailed close-up images of each maximum likelihood threshold are provided in Suppl. <sentence_start/>Figures S1-S9.Fig. 2

Language development

All variables concerning the language domain, including (a) presence/absence of speech, (b) level of verbal language development (non-verbal/words only/sentences), and (c) timing of first sentences acquisition, shared one maximum likelihood threshold located at 114 kb from the telomere (Tables 3 and 4). <sentence_start/>This threshold is located within the <italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic> gene (Fig. 2, dark green; Suppl. <sentence_start/>Fig. S1A for a detailed view). <sentence_start/>This intragenic peak, paired with the presence of nonverbal patients in all categories, including category 1 (Table 4), indicates that <italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic> plays a major role in verbal language impairment. <sentence_start/>In addition, ROC curves for “presence/absence of speech “ also identify a second peak at 1,059 kb from the telomere (Tables 3 and 4), falling within the <italic toggle="yes">BRD1</italic> gene (Fig. 2, dark green; Suppl. <sentence_start/>Fig. S1B).
Motor function and development

Motor development timing was normal in approximately 40% of our PMS patients and delayed in 50%, whereas autonomous walking has never been acquired by 10% [<citation rid="CR46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s11689-024-09572-7" pmid="39363263" pmcid="PMC11451156" count="1">46</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The timing of motor development is strongly correlated with deletion size (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> < 0.001, Table 3), which alone explains 47.6% of the variance: 24/35 (68.6%) patients with deletions < 3 Mb had normal motor development timing, compared to only 1/28 (3.6%) carrying deletions ≥ 3 Mb (Table 5). <sentence_start/>The maximum likelihood threshold is located in a gene-poor region at 3,039 kb from the telomere (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 2.8 × 10<sup>-4</sup> after Bonferroni’s correction; AUC = 0.86) (Table 3), within the oncogenic lncRNA <italic toggle="yes">EPIC1</italic> and roughly 700 kb away from <italic toggle="yes">TBC1D22A</italic>, the first upstream coding gene (Fig. 2; Suppl. <sentence_start/>Fig. S2).

Both gait and muscle strength, assessed clinically during the neurological examination (see Suppl. <sentence_start/>Table 4 in ref. 46], are significantly correlated with deletion size and display maximum likelihood thresholds with practically superimposable locations, i.e. 5,065 kb and 5,013 kb from the telomere, respectively (Tables 3 and 5). <sentence_start/>The influence of this chromosomal region is especially evident for gait, where all 39 (100%) patients with a deletion size < 5 Mb can walk independently, albeit often with abnormal gait (28/39, 71.8%) while 8/16 (50%) with larger deletions cannot walk independently at all and the remaining 8/16 (50%) display an abnormal gait (Table 5). <sentence_start/>Within or just centromeric to this threshold are located two very important neuronal genes, <italic toggle="yes">ATXN10</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">FBLN1</italic> (Fig. 2 and Suppl. <sentence_start/>Fig. S3A). <sentence_start/>For muscle strength only, a second threshold located at 7,363 kb was identified (Tables 3 and 5), falling within the <italic toggle="yes">MPPED1</italic> gene and 140 kb downstream of <italic toggle="yes">SCUBE1</italic> (Suppl. <sentence_start/>Fig. S3B).

Structural abnormalities on brain MRI

The presence of single or multiple structural brain abnormalities on MRI was strongly associated with deletion size (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> < 0.001, Table 3). <sentence_start/>A detailed distribution of specific structural abnormalities by deletion size category is provided in Suppl. <sentence_start/>Table 1. <sentence_start/>The minimum P-value method and/or ROC curves identified three maximum likelihood thresholds, located at 451 kb, 833 kb, and 5,024 kb, respectively (Fig. 2). <sentence_start/>The importance of these three thresholds is clear when considering patient distributions in Table 7: multiple brain structural anomalies are present in 6/24 (25.0%) patients carrying deletions < 1 Mb (categories 1 and 2), 6/16 (37.5%) with deletion size 1-4.99 Mb (categories 3-6), and 18/20 (90.0%) with deletions ≥ 5 Mb (categories 7-11) (Table 7, see Suppl. <sentence_start/>Table 1). <sentence_start/>Similarly, 8/12 (66.7%) cases with an MRI devoid of any evident structural abnormality carry very small deletions, i.e. < 132 kb (Table 7, Suppl. <sentence_start/>Table 1).

Renal and upper urinary malformations

Malformations of the kidney or upper urinary tract, assessed by abdominal ultrasound, were found in approximately one third of our sample, as previously reported [<citation rid="CR46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s11689-024-09572-7" pmid="39363263" pmcid="PMC11451156" count="1">46</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This phenotypic feature was significantly associated with deletion size (Table 3). <sentence_start/>Our results show that renal and upper urinary malformations are present in a small minority (4/32, 12.5%) of patients carrying deletions < 3 Mb in size, increase among patients with deletions of 3-5 Mb (2/8, 25%), and become common among carriers of deletions greater than 5 Mb (11/18, 61.1%) (Table 7). <sentence_start/>Four patients (6.9%) found to carry kidney stones in the absence of upper urinary tract malformations were included in Table 7, two in category 1 (deletion size < 132 kb) and two in category 5 (3-3.99 Mb). <sentence_start/>Two significant deletion thresholds were found for renal abnormalities, the first located at 2,953 kb, and the second at 4,743 kb (Table 3, Fig. 2, Suppl. <sentence_start/>Figures 7 A and 7B). <sentence_start/>The first threshold is located in a relatively gene-poor region and falls into the distal sequence of the longer isoforms of the oncogenic lncRNA <italic toggle="yes">EPIC1</italic> (Fig. 2, Suppl. <sentence_start/>Figure 7 A). <sentence_start/>It is only 86 kb telomeric from the maximum likelihood threshold strongly associated with motor development timing (Fig. 2, Suppl. <sentence_start/>Fig. S2). <sentence_start/>Also the second threshold falls into a chromosomal region encompassing long noncoding RNAs (PRR34, MIRLET7BHG) and a cluster of antisense RNA (Fig. 2, Suppl. <sentence_start/>Figure 7B). <sentence_start/>Further downstream, at 128.6 kb, is located the <italic toggle="yes">WNT7B</italic> gene, which is highly expressed in the urinary tract and is involved in patterning during embryogenesis (see Discussion).
Dysmorphisms

We detected a very significant correlation between deletion size and the presence of dysmorphisms (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> < 0.001, Table 3). <sentence_start/>Deletions smaller than 2 Mb were characterized by 17/28 (60.7%) cases displaying no noticeable dysmorphism and by the complete absence of major dysmorphisms (Table 7). <sentence_start/>Instead, starting from the 2.0-2.9 Mb category onward, the opposite trend was observed, namely only 2/25 (8.0%) cases display no dysmorphism and 8/25 (32.0%) display major dysmorphisms (Table 7). <sentence_start/>Statistical analyses detect a single maximum likelihood threshold at 1,860 kb (Fig. 2, Suppl. <sentence_start/>Fig. S8), beyond which deletions are associated with an increased frequency and severity of dysmorphisms. <sentence_start/>The first coding gene beyond this threshold is <italic toggle="yes">TAFA5</italic>, located at 236 kb (Suppl. <sentence_start/>Fig. S8).
Psychiatric comorbidities: lifetime diagnosis of bipolar disorder

PMS is associated with an increased prevalence of bipolar disorder, which is a frequent cause of regression in adolescents and young adults [<citation rid="CR22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2147/NDT.S30506" pmid="22570549" pmcid="PMC3346055" count="1">22</citation>-<citation rid="CR25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s11689-020-9309-6" pmid="32050889" pmcid="PMC7014655" count="1">25</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Also in our sample, as many as 12/63 (19.0%) PMS patients have received a lifetime diagnosis of bipolar disorder (Table 1). <sentence_start/>A small deletion involving only <italic toggle="yes">RABL2B</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">ACR</italic> and variable segments of <italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic> is present in the majority (7/12, 58.3%) of these PMS patients, while only 5/12 (41.7%) carry larger deletions (Table 8). <sentence_start/>Furthermore, among the 16 patients carrying small deletions (i.e., < 110 kb), those with a comorbid diagnosis of bipolar disorder represent a sizable minority (7/16 = 43.8%) (Table 8). <sentence_start/>Not surprisingly, both the 67 kb and the 114 kb maximum likelihood thresholds are extremely close or fall within the <italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic> gene (Fig. 2, Suppl. <sentence_start/>Fig. S9), similarly to the threshold already presented for language development (Fig. 2, Suppl. <sentence_start/>Figure 1A). <sentence_start/>Finally, this phenotype displays the smallest associated region among our fourteen variables, spanning from 43 kb to 1.531 Mb (Table 3). <sentence_start/>Hence collectively also for bipolar disorder, <italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic> appears to play a major role, possibly without requiring contributions by other genes.
Prediction of functional impact for haploinsufficiency at the proposed candidate genes

The functional impact of haploinsufficiency for the most promising candidates genes was assessed using computational damage prediction scores, namely pLI [<citation rid="CR67" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nature19057" pmid="27535533" pmcid="PMC5018207" count="1">67</citation>], LOEUF [<citation rid="CR68" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-020-2308-7" pmid="32461654" pmcid="PMC7334197" count="1">68</citation>], and pHaplo [<citation rid="CR69" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2022.06.036" pmid="35917817" pmcid="PMC9742861" count="1">69</citation>], in addition to integrating also empirical data on transcriptional sensitivity to haploinsufficiency from the blood transcriptomic study by Breen et al., [<citation rid="CR70" ref-type="bibr" pmid="36276299" doi="10.1016/j.xhgg.2022.100145" pmcid="PMC9579712" count="1">70</citation>] (Table 9). <sentence_start/>Most candidate genes have a low pLI, with the only exception of <italic toggle="yes">BRD1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">FBLN1</italic>, displaying a pLI > 0.9 compatible with intolerance to loss-of-function by this metric (Table 9). <sentence_start/>Importantly, the pLI of the established disease modifier <italic toggle="yes">CELSR1</italic>, associated with lymphedema in PMS [<citation rid="CR13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/cge.14364" pmid="37232218" count="1">13</citation>], is 0 according to gnomAD 4.1.0 (Table 9), confirming the frequent occurance of false-negatives with this metric [<citation rid="CR71" ref-type="bibr" pmid="30977936" doi="10.1002/humu.23763" count="1">71</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In addition to <italic toggle="yes">BRD1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">FBLN1,</italic> LOEUF also detected the well-known morphogenetic gene <italic toggle="yes">PLXNB2</italic> as a constrained gene, and confirmed <italic toggle="yes">CELSR1</italic> (Table 9). <sentence_start/>Instead, pHaplo and the blood transcriptomic data from Breen et al. [<citation rid="CR70" ref-type="bibr" pmid="36276299" doi="10.1016/j.xhgg.2022.100145" pmcid="PMC9579712" count="1">70</citation>], two parameters better fit to predict gene dosage sensitivity for pathomorphic non-pathogenic genes spanning CNVs, indicated that all the candidate genes proposed in the present study either have pHaplo ≥ 0.86 or are dosage-sensitive at the transcriptional level, except for <italic toggle="yes">DENND6B</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">UPK3A</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">MPPED1,</italic> which are not expressed in blood and for which we thus have no information (Table 9). <sentence_start/>This analysis lends support to gene dosage sensitivity for the candidate genes most compatible with our maximum likelihood threshold, especially if they are considered in the context of a large deletion (pHaplo), or if assessed at the transcriptional level [<citation rid="CR70" ref-type="bibr" pmid="36276299" doi="10.1016/j.xhgg.2022.100145" pmcid="PMC9579712" count="1">70</citation>].
Discussion

The ultimate purpose of this study is to explore the heuristic potential of genetic information provided by array-based technologies, in fostering more reliable prognostic predictions and better clinical management of PMS patients carrying chromosome 22q13 deletions. <sentence_start/>This effort follows our long-standing interest toward expanding the role of genetics beyond the narrow boundaries of the diagnostic process of neurodevelopmental disorders, into “actionable genomics” in clinical practice [<citation rid="CR72" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/genes13020323" pmid="35205368" pmcid="PMC8872067" count="1">72</citation>]. <sentence_start/>To this aim, here we first define a set of clinical variables significantly associated with chromosome 22q13 terminal deletion size, and then we analyze their genotype-phenotype correlation. <sentence_start/>Our results support the role of several strong candidate genes in shaping the clinical presentation and developmental trajectory of individuals with PMS, in conjunction with and in addition to <italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic>. <sentence_start/>These candidate genes seemingly influence several clinically-relevant functional domains.
