doi="10.1097/YPG.0b013e328341e069" pmid="21378602" count="1">78</citation>, <citation rid="CR79" ref-type="bibr" pmid="34188957" doi="10.1155/2021/6634584" pmcid="PMC8195663" count="1">79</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Imaging studies using DTI have documented altered myelination in the inferior frontal occipital fasciculus and in the uncinate fasciculus [<citation rid="CR80" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/acn3.50959" pmid="31788990" pmcid="PMC6952316" count="1">80</citation>], the former critical for semantic processing, reading, and basic naming [<citation rid="CR81" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neuroscience.2017.09.011" pmid="28918257" count="1">81</citation>], and the latter for language comprehension, long-term memory, and general speech performance [<citation rid="CR73" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41431-020-00761-1" pmid="33293697" pmcid="PMC8115660" count="1">73</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In mice, reduced expression of <italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic> was correlated with similar myelination abnormalities [<citation rid="CR80" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/acn3.50959" pmid="31788990" pmcid="PMC6952316" count="1">80</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Also <italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic> indels mutant macaques exhibit reduced vocalizations, in addition to repetitive behaviors and abnormal social interactions [<citation rid="CR82" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-019-1278-0" pmid="31189958" count="1">82</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Hence, this first threshold is not surprising, given pivotal role of <italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic> in neurodevelopment, synaptogenesis, and synaptic management [<citation rid="CR83" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nrn.2016.183" pmid="28179641" count="1">83</citation>].

On the other hand, our sample distributions (Table 4) and the second maximum likelihood threshold for verbal language impairment located at 1,059 kb, falling within the candidate gene <italic toggle="yes">BRD1</italic> (Fig. 2, Suppl. <sentence_start/>Figure 1B)<italic toggle="yes">,</italic> demonstrate that deletions greater than 1 Mb in size are already almost invariably associated with absent verbal language, previously linked to larger deletions exceeding 5 Mb [<citation rid="CR74" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ejmg.2023.104745" pmid="36871884" count="1">74</citation>, <citation rid="CR75" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fgene.2022.652454" pmid="35495150" pmcid="PMC9044489" count="1">75</citation>, <citation rid="CR77" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41525-017-0035-2" pmid="29263841" pmcid="PMC5677962" count="1">77</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Interestingly, <italic toggle="yes">BRD1</italic> (OMIM*604,589) encodes for a scaffold protein implicated in chromatin remodeling through histone H3K14 acetylation [<citation rid="CR39" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ajmg.a.62222" pmid="33949759" pmcid="PMC8251815" count="1">39</citation>]; recently, <italic toggle="yes">BRD1</italic> deletion in patients with PMS was associated with a disruption of histone acetylation processes followed by DNA hypermethylation, supporting its crucial role as an epigenetic regulator [<citation rid="CR84" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13148-020-00990-7" pmid="33407854" pmcid="PMC7789817" count="1">84</citation>]. <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">BRD1</italic> is highly expressed in the brain, it is actively involved in neurodevelopment, and the haploinsufficient <italic toggle="yes">Brd1</italic> +/− mice exhibit different neurochemistry and altered synaptic morphology, leading to behavioral and cognitive impairment [<citation rid="CR85" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nbd.2018.12.011" pmid="30590179" count="1">85</citation>, <citation rid="CR86" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nlm.2017.03.009" pmid="28341151" count="1">86</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, <italic toggle="yes">Brd1</italic><sup>+/−</sup> female mice show decreased level of cortical serotonin and of striatal dopamine, leading to depression-like behaviors in the presence of environmental risk factors (e.g. sex and stress) [<citation rid="CR87" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41398-020-00914-2" pmid="32681022" pmcid="PMC7367888" count="1">87</citation>, <citation rid="CR88" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.euroneuro.2012.01.005" pmid="22341945" count="1">88</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Indeed <italic toggle="yes">BRD1</italic> gene variants have been consistently associated with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder [<citation rid="CR89" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ajmg.10191" pmid="11857589" count="1">89</citation>-<citation rid="CR91" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13073-016-0308-x" pmid="27142060" pmcid="PMC4855718" count="1">91</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The DNA methylation and the metabolic profile of PMS patients carrying deletions encompassing <italic toggle="yes">BRD1</italic> are significantly different from those of patients carrying smaller deletions and are clearly altered (e.g. reduced energy production, decreased adaptation to metabolic conditions, and an abnormal reaction to hormones and cytokines), affecting also the expression of genes located outside the chromosome 22q deleted region and in other chromosomes [<citation rid="CR84" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13148-020-00990-7" pmid="33407854" pmcid="PMC7789817" count="1">84</citation>, <citation rid="CR92" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/genes13030528" pmid="35328081" pmcid="PMC8950073" count="1">92</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Hence epigenetic alterations resulting from <italic toggle="yes">BRD1</italic>-spanning deletions could well contribute additively or synergically to increase phenotypic severity in combination with <italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic> and with other genes involved in language delay and in other phenotypes, like seizures [<citation rid="CR93" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/genes14111998" pmid="38002941" pmcid="PMC10671420" count="1">93</citation>] and coincidence of an infectious disease at behavioral symptom onset (see Results).
Motor development and function

Delayed motor development resulting in impaired motor skills (fine more than gross) is almost consistently present in PMS [<citation rid="CR1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/1096-8628(20010615)101:2<91::aid-ajmg1340>3.0.co;2-c" pmid="11391650" count="1">1</citation>-<citation rid="CR3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/2040-2392-4-18" pmid="23758760" pmcid="PMC3707861" count="1">3</citation>]<bold>.</bold> <sentence_start/>Larger deletions have been previously associated with greater developmental delay and motor impairment [<citation rid="CR16" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00439-014-1423-7" pmid="24481935" count="1">16</citation>, <citation rid="CR19" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/jmedgenet-2011-100225" pmid="21984749" count="1">19</citation>, <citation rid="CR42" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s11689-021-09370-5" pmid="34246244" pmcid="PMC8272382" count="1">42</citation>, <citation rid="CR43" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/gim.2013.144" pmid="24136618" count="1">43</citation>, <citation rid="CR94" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ccell.2018.03.006" pmid="29622465" pmcid="PMC6143179" count="1">94</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The majority of our patients with deletion sizes inferior to 3 Mb display normal motor development timing (Table 5). <sentence_start/>In contrast, almost all patients with deletions greater than 3 Mb exhibit delayed motor milestones (Table 5). <sentence_start/>In our cohort, the 3,039 kb maximum likelihood threshold best discriminating patients with normal vs delayed motor development timing falls into the long non-coding RNA (LncRNA) <italic toggle="yes">EPIC1</italic> (Fig. 2, Suppl. <sentence_start/>Figure 2), a well-known cancer-promoting lncRNA able to stimulate cell proliferation and inhibit apoptosis by binding to MYC [<citation rid="CR95" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.18632/aging.102545" pmid="31812951" pmcid="PMC6932932" count="1">95</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In vitro, <italic toggle="yes">EPIC1</italic> expression and MYC binding preserve neuronal cells from oxidative damage [<citation rid="CR96" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.celrep.2019.05.033" pmid="31291588" pmcid="PMC6639060" count="1">96</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Currently available evidence could potentially support roles of <italic toggle="yes">EPIC1</italic> in other features associated with PMS, such as cognitive regression and macrocephaly, more than delayed motor development. <sentence_start/>Instead, a relevant role may be more likely for <italic toggle="yes">TBC1D22A</italic>, the first coding gene located upstream of the 3,039 kb threshold for delayed motor development timing (Table 5, Fig. 2, Suppl. <sentence_start/>Figure 2). <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">TBC1D22A</italic> is expressed in brain and encodes an important regulator of cell surface trafficking for G-protein-coupled receptors, probably acting as a GTPase-activating protein for Rab family protein [<citation rid="CR97" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/1471-2156-14-93" pmid="24067191" pmcid="PMC3851042" count="1">97</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Interestingly, this gene has been identified as a recessive cause of febrile seizures plus [<citation rid="CR98" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/cge.14074" pmid="34664257" count="1">98</citation>] and its locus has been linked to risk of seizures in PMS [<citation rid="CR99" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/pcn.12645" pmid="29430824" count="1">99</citation>]. <sentence_start/>It also frequently spans interstitial deletions in several patients with SHANK-unrelated PMS [<citation rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ajmg.a.36513" pmid="24700646" count="1">36</citation>, <citation rid="CR37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13023-022-02180-5" pmid="35093143" pmcid="PMC8800328" count="1">37</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Finally, CpG islands regulating <italic toggle="yes">TBC1D22A</italic> expression are hypermethylated in patients with bipolar disorder (BD) and hypomethylated in patients with SCZ [<citation rid="CR100" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/08830738231204395" pmid="37849292" count="1">100</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Collectively, these results point strongly toward <italic toggle="yes">TBC1D22A</italic> as playing a pivotal role in motor development timing and, more broadly, in the structure and function of CNS neural networks, also in terms of excitation/inhibition imbalance. <sentence_start/>In addition to deletion size, it will be interesting to search for possible epigenetic modifications in the non-deleted allele in patients with haploinsufficient regions encompassing this gene.

Gait and muscle strength are often impaired in PMS [<citation rid="CR1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/1096-8628(20010615)101:2<91::aid-ajmg1340>3.0.co;2-c" pmid="11391650" count="1">1</citation>-<citation rid="CR4" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13229-018-0205-9" pmid="29719671" pmcid="PMC5921983" count="1">4</citation>, <citation rid="CR46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s11689-024-09572-7" pmid="39363263" pmcid="PMC11451156" count="1">46</citation>, <citation rid="CR101" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/79911" pmid="11017075" count="1">101</citation>]. <sentence_start/>They are also significantly affected by deletion length, as documented in a previous [<citation rid="CR94" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ccell.2018.03.006" pmid="29622465" pmcid="PMC6143179" count="1">94</citation>] and in the present study (Table 3). <sentence_start/>For example, lack of autonomous walking is observed in our sample only among carriers of deletions greater than 5 Mb (Table 5). <sentence_start/>Based on our analysis, both these functions are affected by genes located at or just beyond a 5,013 kb threshold, with the most likely candidates represented by <italic toggle="yes">ATXN10</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">FBLN1</italic> (Fig. 2, Suppl. <sentence_start/>Fig. S3). <sentence_start/>The <italic toggle="yes">ATXN10</italic> gene is highly expressed in the brain especially during gestation and its expression decreases after birth, consistently with a crucial role in CNS development [<citation rid="CR39" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ajmg.a.62222" pmid="33949759" pmcid="PMC8251815" count="1">39</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Initially the expansion of a pentanucleotide ATTCT repeat located in intron 9 has been identified as the cause of spinocerebellar ataxia-10 (SCA-10) [<citation rid="CR102" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fcell.2021.705182" pmid="34970537" pmcid="PMC8712648" count="1">102</citation>]. <sentence_start/>More recently, a broader morphogenetic role has been recognized [<citation rid="CR103" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ajmg.a.38559" pmid="29193617" count="1">103</citation>] and <italic toggle="yes">ATXN10</italic> haploinsufficiency has been proposed as a possible contributor to the neurodevelopmental phenotype of 22q13.31 microdeletion syndrome, caused by interstitial microdeletions involving <italic toggle="yes">ATXN10</italic> while sparing <italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic> [<citation rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ajmg.a.36513" pmid="24700646" count="1">36</citation>, <citation rid="CR104" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s0378-1119(97)00149-2" pmid="9266672" count="1">104</citation>, <citation rid="CR105" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00213-023-06355-1" pmid="36939856" count="1">105</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Previous studies have proposed that, in addition to altered neurodevelopment due to both <italic toggle="yes">ATXN10</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">FBLN1</italic> haploinsufficiency, further contributions to gait deficits in patients with deleted <italic toggle="yes">FBLN1</italic> may stem from hand/feet dysmorphisms (large or fleshy hands), as this gene has been conclusively associated with Synpolydactyly-2 (OMIM n. 608,180) [<citation rid="CR104" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s0378-1119(97)00149-2" pmid="9266672" count="1">104</citation>, <citation rid="CR105" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00213-023-06355-1" pmid="36939856" count="1">105</citation>].

In addition to this first threshold detecting <italic toggle="yes">ATXN10</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">FBLN1</italic>, a second threshold located at 7,363 kb points toward <italic toggle="yes">MPPED1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">SCUBE1</italic> as additional contributors to reduced muscle strength (Table 5, Fig. 2, Suppl. <sentence_start/>Fig. S3B). <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">MPPED1</italic> (metallo-phosphoesterase domain containing protein 1) is highly expressed in the human fetal brain [<citation rid="CR105" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00213-023-06355-1" pmid="36939856" count="1">105</citation>] and reduced expression yields cognitive impairment in ovariectomized mice [<citation rid="CR106" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1074/jbc.M805996200" pmid="19004815" count="1">106</citation>]. <sentence_start/>It modulates the development and function of neocortical and hippocampal neurons through its metallo-phosphodiesterase activity [<citation rid="CR107" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12929-023-00925-3" pmid="37237303" pmcid="PMC10214685" count="1">107</citation>]. <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">SCUBE1</italic> (Signal Peptide-CUB-EGF Domain-Containing Protein 1) is a morphogenetic gene expressed in different tissues, including the brain, kidney, platelets and endothelial cells [<citation rid="CR108" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/jez.b.21260" pmid="19101956" count="1">108</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Homozygous <italic toggle="yes">Scube1</italic><italic toggle="yes"><sup>Δcub/Δcub</sup></italic>mice lacking the CR and CUB domain display acrania, exencephaly, and death shortly after birth demonstrating the major role of this gene in early craniofacial development [<citation rid="CR109" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.biopsych.2019.09.029" pmid="31771860" pmcid="PMC7160031" count="1">109</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Rare de novo disruptive <italic toggle="yes">SCUBE1</italic> missense variants have been found in patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder [<citation rid="CR110" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/1866-1955-6-39" pmid="25784960" pmcid="PMC4362650" count="1">110</citation>].

While the first threshold detects strong candidate genes supported by multiple converging lines of evidence, to our knowledge this is the first study suggesting a possible association between the latter chromosomal region and reduced muscle strength. <sentence_start/>Given our limited sample size, despite reaching statistical significance (Table 3), this finding should be viewed especially with caution, until replicated in additional cohorts of PMS patients.
Social cognition (eye contact, exchange gesture, joint attention)

Autism is frequently diagnosed among PMS patients, with prevalence estimates ranging from less than 30% to more than 80%, possibly higher among <italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic> mutation carriers and in patients with very small deletions [<citation rid="CR1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/1096-8628(20010615)101:2<91::aid-ajmg1340>3.0.co;2-c" pmid="11391650" count="1">1</citation>-<citation rid="CR4" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13229-018-0205-9" pmid="29719671" pmcid="PMC5921983" count="1">4</citation>, <citation rid="CR29" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ejhg.2012.175" pmid="22892527" pmcid="PMC3573207" count="1">29</citation>-<citation rid="CR34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1086/522590" pmid="17999366" pmcid="PMC2276348" count="1">34</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Compared with prior literature, rates of ASD are relatively low both in our overall sample (28.6%) [<citation rid="CR46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s11689-024-09572-7" pmid="39363263" pmcid="PMC11451156" count="1">46</citation>] and in our patients carrying chromosome 22q deletions (25.4%) (Table 1). <sentence_start/>The partially overlapping clinical features of profound intellectual disability (ID) and severe ASD (for example, intense stereotypic behaviors are often present in both conditions), the use of ADOS scores instead of clinical DSM-5 criteria as primary measure to define the presence of ASD (ADOS is often positive when administered to individuals with profound ID), and an insufficient focus on the psychopathological foundations distinguishing ID from ASD (cognitive development congruent with an earlier age in ID vs primary interest in objects at the expense of social cognition and interactions in ASD) could explain the variability in ASD prevalence estimates reported in different studies [<citation rid="CR46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s11689-024-09572-7" pmid="39363263" pmcid="PMC11451156" count="1">46</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Hence, in our genotype-phenotype correlation analysis, rather than using a categorical diagnostic approach, we focused on eye contact, reciprocal object exchange gesture, and joint attention, as elicited and observed by the clinician visiting each PMS patient. <sentence_start/>Eye contact, exchange gesture, and joint attention in the present context should not be viewed as a “proxy” for an ASD diagnosis, because they can be variably compromised also in individuals with profound Intellectual Disability who do not deserve a primary or co-morbid ASD diagnosis. <sentence_start/>This likely explains the apparent discrepancy between relatively low rates of an ASD diagnosis (Table 1) and higher numbers of patients displaying partial or severe deficits in these three parameters (Table 6).

These three social behaviors were all significantly correlated with deletion size and all converged upon the same threshold located at 3,282 kb (Tables 3 and 6), almost superimposable to the threshold located at 3,039 kb critical for motor development timing (Table 3). <sentence_start/>Deletions smaller than 3 Mb show a relatively even distribution, possibly with a slight predominance of normal vs dysfunctional phenotypes (Table 6). <sentence_start/>Instead, the majority of patients carrying deletions larger than 3 Mb show no exchange gesture and joint attention, while eye contact becomes mostly inconsistent (Table 6). <sentence_start/>This threshold again falls within the <italic toggle="yes">TBC1D22A</italic> gene (Fig. 2, Suppl. <sentence_start/>Fig. S4), already discussed in reference to motor developmental delay (see above). <sentence_start/>This consistency among different behavioral parameters interconnected with social cognition is indeed reassuring and supports the validity of this finding<italic toggle="yes">.</italic>

Apparently less penetrant as compared to the first threshold is a second threshold located at 4,743 kb, reaching nominal significance only for joint attention (Tables 3 and 6). <sentence_start/>We cannot exclude this threshold may also apply to eye contact and exchange gesture, but statistical power may be insufficient in our sample to detect this signal. <sentence_start/>This second threshold overlaps with the one identified for renal abnormalities (Suppl. <sentence_start/>Fig S7B). <sentence_start/>It falls within a cluster of long non-coding RNAs and miRNAs, but it may also point again at <italic toggle="yes">ATXN10</italic> and/or <italic toggle="yes">FBLN1</italic>, which are located only 260 and 500 kb upstream (see below).
Infectious disease at onset of behavioral manifestations

In approximately half of our PMS patients, who do not display severe muscle hypotonia soon after birth, parents reported noticing initial motor and behavioral manifestations of PMS in concomitance with an infectious episode, usually an ear infection, a bronchitis or an infection of the upper airways [<citation rid="CR46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s11689-024-09572-7" pmid="39363263" pmcid="PMC11451156" count="1">46</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, patients with PMS frequently exhibit immune dysfunction, fostering recurrent infections, as well as asthma, food allergies, and atopic dermatitis [<citation rid="CR3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/2040-2392-4-18" pmid="23758760" pmcid="PMC3707861" count="1">3</citation>, <citation rid="CR7" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ajmg.a.33253" pmcid="PMC3119894" pmid="20186804" count="1">7</citation>, <citation rid="CR111" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ejmg.2010.06.004" pmid="20541044" count="1">111</citation>, <citation rid="CR112" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fimmu.2023.1203848" pmid="37475860" pmcid="PMC10355154" count="1">112</citation>]. <sentence_start/>We identified two peaks related to dysimmunity. <sentence_start/>The first is located at 253 kb and falls next to two immune-relevant loci, namely <italic toggle="yes">KLHDC7B</italic> and its lncRNA <italic toggle="yes">KLHDC7B-DT</italic>, as well as <italic toggle="yes">CIMAP1B</italic> (Fig. 2, Suppl. <sentence_start/>Fig. S5). <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">KLHDC7B-DT</italic> has been identified as one of the lncRNAs most contributing to lupus nephritic activity, acting as a key regulator of interferon-mediated processes and B-cell adaptive immunity [<citation rid="CR113" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/1878-0261.12446" pmid="30648789" pmcid="PMC6441920" count="1">113</citation>]. <sentence_start/>A reduced expression of the same lncRNA and of <italic toggle="yes">KLHDC7B</italic>, as would be predicted to occur in the presence of haploinsufficiency, can result in increased cellular migration and invasion, as well as resistance to apoptosis in breast cancer cells [<citation rid="CR114" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1155/2021/2676996" pmid="34630563" pmcid="PMC8497127" count="1">114</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Finally, <italic toggle="yes">KLHDC7B</italic> is one of only eight TNF family member genes which contribute to the prognostic risk score for adenopancreatic carcinoma, by determining the immunomodulatory response of the host to cancer [<citation rid="CR115" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00404-022-06805-9" pmid="36217035" count="1">115</citation>]. <sentence_start/>On the other hand, the expression of <italic toggle="yes">CIMAP1B</italic> is correlated with M1 macrophage infiltration affecting placental development and the immunoregulation of fetal growth restriction [<citation rid="CR116" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.62347/GHKF1995" pmid="38590411" pmcid="PMC10998755" count="1">116</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This gene is highly expressed in the brain [<citation rid="CR116" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.62347/GHKF1995" pmid="38590411" pmcid="PMC10998755" count="1">116</citation>], and was also found implicated in glioma proliferation and apoptosis through the JAK/STAT pathway, critical for immune regulation processes [<citation rid="CR117" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/brain/awu408" pmid="25665584" count="1">117</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Most importantly, it is strongly associated with T cell pathology in multiple sclerosis and significantly downregulated in T<sub>H</sub>17 cells during the course of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis [<citation rid="CR118" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ncomms6872" pmid="25519988" pmcid="PMC4490789" count="1">118</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Hence, <italic toggle="yes">CIMAP1B</italic> haploinsufficiency could well contribute to an aggressive neuroinflammation in the CNS.

The second threshold, located at 1,059 kb, fully overlaps with the second threshold concerning verbal language, as discussed above, and falls within the <italic toggle="yes">BRD1</italic> gene (Fig. 2, Suppl. <sentence_start/>Figure 1B). <sentence_start/>By acting as an epigenetic regulator, <italic toggle="yes">BRD1</italic> can seemingly produce chromatin changes significantly affecting not only neurodevelopment, but also immune function. <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">BRD1</italic> has been identified as a key gene in promoting CD8 expression in developing thymocytes evolving toward the NK phenotype [<citation rid="CR119" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12891-022-06098-8" pmid="36550476" pmcid="PMC9783407" count="1">119</citation>]. <sentence_start/>It is the strongest <italic toggle="yes">in silico</italic> candidate to explain immune infiltration in osteoarthritis [<citation rid="CR120" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/0008-5472.CAN-20-1674" pmid="33158814" pmcid="PMC7878408" count="1">120</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Its downregulation activates NK and CD8 T cells to transition from inert to more active and cytotoxic phenotypes [<citation rid="CR121" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/10738584241252576" pmid="38712859" count="1">121</citation>]: this effect may indeed be helpful in enhancing the efficacy of immunotherapy for various forms of infiltrating tumors [<citation rid="CR121" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/10738584241252576" pmid="38712859" count="1">121</citation>], but could instead promote excessive neuroinflammation in the PMS brain.

Collectively, the evidence summarized above points toward <italic toggle="yes">KLHDC7B</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">KLHDC7B-DT</italic>, and especially <italic toggle="yes">CIMAP1B</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">BRD1</italic> as strong candidates for dysimmunity in PMS, outlining a plausible explanation for the worsening of behavioral and motor deficits coincident with infections in early infancy, as reported by the parents of many children with deletions involving these genes. <sentence_start/>In the most plausible scenario, peripheral immune activation would reverberate to the CNS, sparking central neuroinflammation ultimately leading to excessive synaptic pruning by activated microglia, responsible for motor and cognitive regression [<citation rid="CR122" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fnins.2023.1125428" pmid="37021129" pmcid="PMC10067592" count="1">122</citation>, <citation rid="CR123" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/genes13030504" pmid="35328058" pmcid="PMC8955098" count="1">123</citation>].
Structural abnormalities found in brain MRI

Abnormal brain MRI have been extensively reported in patients with PMS, both in <italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic>-related and in <italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic>-unrelated PMS [<citation rid="CR3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/2040-2392-4-18" pmid="23758760" pmcid="PMC3707861" count="1">3</citation>, <citation rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ajmg.a.36513" pmid="24700646" count="1">36</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Reduced myelination, thin corpus callosum, global atrophy of white matter, brain asymmetry, reduced myelination and hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis have been frequently reported [<citation rid="CR7" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ajmg.a.33253" pmcid="PMC3119894" pmid="20186804" count="1">7</citation>, <citation rid="CR8" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1542/peds.2007-2584" pmid="18625665" count="1">8</citation>, <citation rid="CR77" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41525-017-0035-2" pmid="29263841" pmcid="PMC5677962" count="1">77</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Positron emission study (PET) showed a localized dysfunction of the left temporal pole and significant amygdala hypoperfusion in eight children with PMS, with normal structural brain MRI o just with thinning of the corpus callosum [<citation rid="CR8" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1542/peds.2007-2584" pmid="18625665" count="1">8</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In our sample, 48/60 (80%) of PMS patients display at least one structural abnormality on brain MRI, while 30/60 (50%) display two or more [<citation rid="CR46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s11689-024-09572-7" pmid="39363263" pmcid="PMC11451156" count="1">46</citation>] (Table 7; for specific brain anomalies see Suppl. <sentence_start/>Table S1). <sentence_start/>In the present study, three thresholds located at 451 kb, 833 kb and 5,024 kb from the 22q telomeric end were found to reach statistical significance (Table 3, Fig. 2). <sentence_start/>The 451 kb threshold falls into the first intron of the <italic toggle="yes">PPP6R2</italic> gene, just telomeric to <italic toggle="yes">DENND6B</italic> (Suppl. <sentence_start/>Fig. S6A). <sentence_start/>Both these genes do not appear as strong candidates to yield structural anomalies in the CNS, although both are expressed in the brain and cannot be entirely excluded. <sentence_start/>The morphogenetic gene <italic toggle="yes">PLXNB2</italic> (OMIM*604,263), located immediately centromeric to <italic toggle="yes">DENND6B</italic> and only 50 kb upstream of this first threshold, represents a much stronger candidate (Suppl. <sentence_start/>Fig. S6A). <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">PLXNB2</italic> exerts multiple roles in cerebral, cerebellar, and kidney development [<citation rid="CR39" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ajmg.a.62222" pmid="33949759" pmcid="PMC8251815" count="1">39</citation>]. <sentence_start/>It encodes for one of the Plexins, large transmembrane cell surface receptors able to control cell migration and axon guidance by binding semaphorins. <sentence_start/>It is involved in the closure of the neural tube [<citation rid="CR124" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.5381-06.2007" pmid="17554007" pmcid="PMC6672150" count="1">124</citation>], in the proliferation and migration of cerebellar granule cell precursors, in cell migration and differentiation during corticogenesis, and in the formation of excitatory synapses in hippocampal neurons [<citation rid="CR10" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ajmg.a.35700" pmcid="PMC3733662" pmid="23225497" count="1">10</citation>, <citation rid="CR124" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.5381-06.2007" pmid="17554007" pmcid="PMC6672150" count="1">124</citation>-<citation rid="CR126" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.mcn.2018.06.008" pmid="29981480" pmcid="PMC6191356" count="1">126</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In addition to the CNS, also the developing kidney expresses <italic toggle="yes">PLXNB2</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">PLXNB2</italic>-/- mice display kidney and urinary tract malformations [<citation rid="CR126" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.mcn.2018.06.008" pmid="29981480" pmcid="PMC6191356" count="1">126</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In fact, Plxnb2 binds Sema4C and spurs the branching of the ureteric epithelium [<citation rid="CR127" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.diff.2010.10.001" pmid="21035938" count="1">127</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Hence, <italic toggle="yes">PLXNB2</italic> has already been proposed as a strong candidate gene for brain and cerebellar MRI phenotypes in PMS [<citation rid="CR10" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ajmg.a.35700" pmcid="PMC3733662" pmid="23225497" count="1">10</citation>], as well as for kidney disorders in patients with 22q13 deletion syndrome [<citation rid="CR128" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00467-023-06146-y" pmid="37733098" count="1">128</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Our results are thus compatible with the proposed association of <italic toggle="yes">PLXNB2</italic>, at least with brain and cerebellar imaging anomalies.

The second threshold is located at 833 kb and the first gene about 50 kb centromeric to this peak is <italic toggle="yes">PIM3</italic> (Suppl. <sentence_start/>Fig. S6B), which encodes for a serine/threonine kinase able to prevent apoptosis and to promote cell survival and protein translation [<citation rid="CR129" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1349-7006.2011.01966.x" pmid="21518143" count="1">129</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In vivo, this gene is expressed in several tissues, including brain, and plays a crucial role in the self-renewal of embryonic stem cells, stimulating cell proliferation [<citation rid="CR130" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1634/stemcells.2007-0066" pmid="17717068" count="1">130</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In rodent brain, <italic toggle="yes">PIM3</italic> is induced in the hippocampus in response to stimuli that elicit long-term potentiation [<citation rid="CR131" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/emboj/18.12.3359" pmid="10369676" pmcid="PMC1171416" count="1">131</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Reduced <italic toggle="yes">PIM3</italic> gene expression can reduce proliferation both in normal and tumor cells [<citation rid="CR129" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1349-7006.2011.01966.x" pmid="21518143" count="1">129</citation>, <citation rid="CR130" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1634/stemcells.2007-0066" pmid="17717068" count="1">130</citation>].

Moving 42.3 kb further upstream from <italic toggle="yes">PIM3</italic> is <italic toggle="yes">ALG12</italic> (Suppl. <sentence_start/>Fig. S6B), another potential candidate gene [<citation rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ajmg.a.36513" pmid="24700646" count="1">36</citation>, <citation rid="CR37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13023-022-02180-5" pmid="35093143" pmcid="PMC8800328" count="1">37</citation>]. <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">ALG12</italic> encodes for an α6-mannosyltransferase and autosomal recessive biallelic inactivation of this gene produces <italic toggle="yes">Congenital Disorder of Glycosylation, Type Ig</italic> (ALG12-CDG) [<citation rid="CR132" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ymgme.2019.08.007" pmid="31481313" count="1">132</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Compound heterozygous disruptive variants in <italic toggle="yes">ALG12</italic> have been reported in two patients with hypoplasia of the cerebrum, brain stem and cerebellar vermis [<citation rid="CR125" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.4710-06.2007" pmid="17409257" pmcid="PMC6672405" count="1">125</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The inactivation of a single allele should not be sufficient to yield brain structural anomalies in PMS patients with chromosome 22q13 deletions and the co-existence of a disruptive mutation located in the non-deleted allele is predicted to be a rare event unable to drive the statistical signal we detect in our sample. <sentence_start/>Conceivably, if the second threshold is not entirely due to <italic toggle="yes">PIM3</italic>, gene x gene interactions involving <italic toggle="yes">ALG12</italic> or contributions by low-function genetic or epigenetic variants may warrant further investigations.

Finally, the third peak is practically superimposable to the threshold involving <italic toggle="yes">ATXN10</italic> in gait, muscle strength and joint attention (Suppl. <sentence_start/>Fig. S6C), as described above. <sentence_start/>This result further points toward the potential relevance of <italic toggle="yes">ATXN10</italic> haploinsufficiency in shaping the PMS phenotype. <sentence_start/>However, a missense mutation, p.(Cys397Phe) in fibulin-1 <italic toggle="yes">(FBLN1)</italic> has been detected in three affected siblings exhibiting brain atrophy and compression of spinal cord on MRI [<citation rid="CR133" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ejhg.2013.210" pmid="24084572" pmcid="PMC3992572" count="1">133</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Hence, once again it is not possible to exclude <italic toggle="yes">FBLN1</italic> contributions also in reference to brain morphology.

Overall, as many as 18/20 (90.0%) patients carrying deletions exceeding 5 Mb display two or more structural abnormalities (Table 7). <sentence_start/>These patients carry deletions encompassing all the candidate genes discussed above (<italic toggle="yes">PIM3</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PLXNB2</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">ALG12</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">ATXN10</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">FBLN1</italic>), while patients carrying larger deletions also suffer from deficits produced by additional known pathogenic genes, like <italic toggle="yes">TCF20</italic> [<citation rid="CR134" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nn.4352" pmid="27479843" count="1">134</citation>-<citation rid="CR136" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ejhg.2016.90" pmid="27436265" pmcid="PMC5117939" count="1">136</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Structural CNS abnormalities are thus likely to result from complex gene x gene, and gene x environment interactions involving multiple major loci located in chr22q13 and involved in brain macroanatomy.

dysplasia, horseshoe kidneys, and pyelectasis have been described in different genotype phenotype studies [<citation rid="CR3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/2040-2392-4-18" pmid="23758760" pmcid="PMC3707861" count="1">3</citation>, <citation rid="CR8" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1542/peds.2007-2584" pmid="18625665" count="1">8</citation>, <citation rid="CR46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s11689-024-09572-7" pmid="39363263" pmcid="PMC11451156" count="1">46</citation>, <citation rid="CR104" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s0378-1119(97)00149-2" pmid="9266672" doi="10.3390/genes13061042" pmid="35741804" pmcid="PMC9223119" count="1">137</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Large deletions have been linked to renal abnormalities, and <italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic> seems to play no role in urinary tract dysfunction [<citation rid="CR4" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13229-018-0205-9" pmid="29719671" pmcid="PMC5921983" count="1">4</citation>, <citation rid="CR14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s11689-019-9273-1" pmcid="PMC6637483" pmid="31319798" count="1">14</citation>, <citation rid="CR137" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/genes13061042" pmid="35741804" pmcid="PMC9223119" count="1">137</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In prior studies, the genes <italic toggle="yes">UPK3A, FBLN1, ZBED4, WNT7B, SCUBE1 RABL2B, PNPLA3, PLXNB2,</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">CELSR1</italic> have been proposed as possibly associated with kidney disorders [<citation rid="CR14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s11689-019-9273-1" pmcid="PMC6637483" pmid="31319798" count="1">14</citation>, <citation rid="CR104" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s0378-1119(97)00149-2" pmid="9266672" count="1">104</citation>, <citation rid="CR128" count="1">137</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In our sample, the prevalence of malformations of the kidney and of the upper urinary tract, or the presence of kidney stones increased considerably with a deletion size greater than 5 Mb (Table 7). <sentence_start/>We identify two maximum likelihood thresholds and both fall in gene-poor regions, enriched in non-coding transcripts, such as EPIC1, PRR34, MIRLET7BHG, and a cluster of antisense RNAs (Suppl. <sentence_start/>Figures 7 A and 7B). <sentence_start/>Genetic variants of the MIRLET7BHG short non-coding RNA (miR) have been associated with cancer [<citation rid="CR138" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41419-021-03494-1" pmid="33771969" pmcid="PMC7997896" count="1">138</citation>] and polycystic ovarian syndrome[<citation rid="CR139" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/cen.14087" pmid="31482638" count="1">139</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In tissues from the prefrontal cortex of the brain of SARS-CoV-2 infected patients, <italic toggle="yes">MIRLET7BHG</italic> was found to be upregulated in excitatory neurons [<citation rid="CR140" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/adbi.202101310" pmcid="PMC9348399" pmid="35661455" count="1">140</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The second threshold may also involve <italic toggle="yes">WNT7B</italic>, in line with previous suggestive evidence [<citation rid="CR128" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00467-023-06146-y" pmid="37733098" count="1">128</citation>, <citation rid="CR137" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/genes13061042" pmid="35741804" pmcid="PMC9223119" count="1">137</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This gene is a member of the WNT gene family, encoding secreted signaling proteins implicated in oncogenesis and in developmental processes, including regulation of cell fate and patterning during embryogenesis; among members of the human WNT family, this gene product is most similar to the WNT7A protein, and is highly expressed in the kidney and urinary tract, where it exerts prominent developmental roles [<citation rid="CR141" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00467-013-2733-z" pmid="24445433" pmcid="PMC3928513" count="1">141</citation>]. toggle="yes">PLXN2B, UPK3A, FBLN1,</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">CELSR1</italic>. <sentence_start/>However, while coding genes have received most attention [<citation rid="CR128" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00467-023-06146-y" pmid="37733098" count="1">128</citation>, <citation rid="CR137" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/genes13061042" pmid="35741804" pmcid="PMC9223119" count="1">137</citation>], our results indicate that the contribution of non-coding RNAs to renal and urinary tract malformations indeed deserve further scrutiny.
Dysmorphisms

PMS patients can exhibit several dysmorphic features, such as large fleshy hands, bulbous nose, long eyelashes, ear malformations, hypoplastic or dysplastic nails, full lips, pointed chin, dolichocephaly, and microcephaly/macrocephaly [<citation rid="CR1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/1096-8628(20010615)101:2<91::aid-ajmg1340>3.0.co;2-c" pmid="11391650" count="1">1</citation>-<citation rid="CR3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/2040-2392-4-18" pmid="23758760" pmcid="PMC3707861" count="1">3</citation>, <citation rid="CR94" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ccell.2018.03.006" pmid="29622465" pmcid="PMC6143179" count="1">94</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In our sample, deletions ≥ 2 Mb were clearly associated with greater incidence and severity of dysmorphic features both minor and major (Table 7). <sentence_start/>Our maximum likelihood threshold indicates <italic toggle="yes">TAFA5</italic> (also named <italic toggle="yes">FAM19A5</italic>) as the strongest candidate (Fig. 2, Suppl. <sentence_start/>Fig. S8). <sentence_start/>This gene is involved in the generation of neural stem cells and oligodendrocyte precursor cells, and acts as a regulator for immune and nervous cells both during development and in response to pathological conditions [<citation rid="CR142" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fnins.2019.00917" pmid="31543758" pmcid="PMC6730007" count="1">142</citation>]. <sentence_start/>It was linked to depressive symptoms, neuroinflammation, neurodegeneration, and cognitive impairment both in humans and mice [<citation rid="CR143" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.bbrc.2019.12.119" pmid="31954515" count="1">143</citation>-<citation rid="CR145" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41380-020-0720-x" pmid="32317715" count="1">145</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, <italic toggle="yes">TAFA5</italic>/<italic toggle="yes">FAM19A5</italic> also inhibits RANKL-induced osteoclast differentiation essential for bone metabolism and homeostasis [<citation rid="CR146" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41598-017-15586-0" pmid="29138422" pmcid="PMC5686125" count="1">146</citation>]. <sentence_start/>While contributions to CNS dysfunction cannot be excluded, this peripheral function as a modulator of osteoclastogenesis and bone remodelling may explain an association with dysmorphic features.
Lifetime diagnosis of bipolar disorder

<italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic> deletion appears to be sufficient in enhancing the risk of co-morbid bipolar disorder. <sentence_start/>This result is in line with previous evidence documenting greater liability toward psychiatric comorbidities (bipolar and unipolar affective disorder, catatonia) in carriers of small deletions and <italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic> point mutations, compared to carriers of large deletions who suffer from more severe cognitive and motor impairment [<citation rid="CR22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2147/NDT.S30506" pmid="22570549" pmcid="PMC3346055" count="1">22</citation>-<citation rid="CR25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s11689-020-9309-6" pmid="32050889" pmcid="PMC7014655" count="1">25</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Conceivably, these comorbidities could occur primarily in the presence of a familial genetic liability toward affective disorders, whose penetrance may be enhanced by the <italic toggle="yes">de novo</italic> haploinsufficiency of <italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic>, but this hypothesis remains to be conclusively demonstrated.
Prediction of functional impact for threshold-adjacent genes

To further test whether the heterozygous deletion of the proposed candidates gene can affect the clinical phenotype, in addition to performing a thorough literature review, we also annotated the most promising candidate genes with computational damage prediction metrics and with empirical data derived from the blood transcriptomic study by Breen et al., [<citation rid="CR70" ref-type="bibr" pmid="36276299" doi="10.1016/j.xhgg.2022.100145" pmcid="PMC9579712" count="1">70</citation>], who contrasted PMS patients with large vs small deletions (Table 9). <sentence_start/>Both pLI [<citation rid="CR67" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nature19057" pmid="27535533" pmcid="PMC5018207" count="1">67</citation>] and LOEUF [<citation rid="CR68" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-020-2308-7" pmid="32461654" pmcid="PMC7334197" count="1">68</citation>] support a very limited number of our candidate genes, especially <italic toggle="yes">BRD1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">FBLN1</italic> (Table 9). <sentence_start/>LOEUF, but not pLI, confirms the known pathomorphic gene <italic toggle="yes">CELSR1</italic> and detects also <italic toggle="yes">PLXNB2</italic> as a constrained gene (Table 9). <sentence_start/>This result is not surprising, because these metrics are sensitive to genetic constraint, i.e. they detect pathogenic disruptive mutations which severely impair fitness [<citation rid="CR147" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41588-019-0383-1" pmid="30962618" pmcid="PMC6615471" count="1">147</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In our context, both pLI and LOEUF display at least two major limitations: (a) their prediction of genetic constraint measures the selective pressure exerted by the disruption of single genes, without taking into account the complex interactions among genes spanning the deleted region in large copy number variants (CNVs) and between these deleted genes and many other genes located in non-deleted chromosomes [<citation rid="CR70" ref-type="bibr" pmid="36276299" doi="10.1016/j.xhgg.2022.100145" pmcid="PMC9579712" count="1">70</citation>]; (b) in large chromosome 22q13 terminal deletions, while <italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic> clearly represents the primary <italic toggle="yes">pathogenic</italic> gene, other genes may well play <italic toggle="yes">pathomorphic</italic> roles in shaping the presence/absence, time course, and severity of specific clinical signs and symptoms, even if they are not “disease causing” <italic toggle="yes">per se</italic>. <sentence_start/>Finally, the pLI is endowed with several known pitfalls and should be interpreted with caution especially when negative [<citation rid="CR71" ref-type="bibr" pmid="30977936" doi="10.1002/humu.23763" count="1">71</citation>]. <sentence_start/>A glaring example is represented here by <italic toggle="yes">CELSR1</italic>, an established disease modifier associated with lymphedema [<citation rid="CR13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/cge.14364" pmid="37232218" count="1">13</citation>] displaying a pLI of 0 according to gnomAD v4.1.0 (Table 9).

To circumvent these limitations, (a) we employed the pHaplo statistics, an ensemble machine-learning score designed to predict the probability of gene dosage sensitivity specifically in CNVs [<citation rid="CR69" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2022.06.036" pmid="35917817" pmcid="PMC9742861" count="1">69</citation>]; and (b) we sought gene dosage transcriptional effects in the blood transcriptomic data set recently produced contrasting PMS patients carrying large vs small deletion [<citation rid="CR70" ref-type="bibr" pmid="36276299" doi="10.1016/j.xhgg.2022.100145" pmcid="PMC9579712" count="1">70</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Using these approaches, all the candidate genes proposed in the present study either yield a pHaplo score ≥ 0.86 or are dosage-sensitive at the transcriptional level, except for <italic toggle="yes">DENND6B</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">UPK3A</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">MPPED1,</italic> which are not expressed in blood. <sentence_start/>This demonstrates that the majority of the candidate genes we identified are indeed dosage-sensitive at the transcriptional level and can be predicted to exert functional effects when in the context of a large deletion, though not necessarily producing severe genetic constraint when haploinsufficient at the single gene level.

The fundamental distinction that needs to be made between “pathogenic” and “pathomorphic” genes in CNV-associated genetic syndromes, the complexity of gene-gene interactions in determining the functional consequences of large CNVs [<citation rid="CR70" ref-type="bibr" pmid="36276299" doi="10.1016/j.xhgg.2022.100145" pmcid="PMC9579712" count="1">70</citation>], as well as the results displayed in Table 9, in our opinion all raise caution into excluding <italic toggle="yes">a priori</italic> candidate genes identified performing empirical genotype-phenotype correlations, based solely on computational predictions. <sentence_start/>Also the existence of rare autosomal recessive conditions may justify the exclusion of disease-causing pathogenic roles for haploinsufficiency at a given locus, but not of pathomorphic contributions to the clinical picture. <sentence_start/>Specifically, the largest chromosome 22q13.3 deleted region in PMS contains 13 genes with well-proven roles in autosomal recessive conditions [<citation rid="CR46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s11689-024-09572-7" pmid="39363263" pmcid="PMC11451156" count="1">46</citation>], with the possible addition of <italic toggle="yes">SCO2</italic> and recently of <italic toggle="yes">PLXNB2</italic> [<citation rid="CR148" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/jmg-2023-109728" pmid="38458752" pmcid="PMC11228227" count="1">148</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Still, especially for morphogenetic genes like <italic toggle="yes">PLXNB2</italic>, our results suggest that their haploinsufficiency, in conjunction with <italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic> haploinsufficiency, may well produce pathomorphic changes specifically in the context of PMS (Table 9). <sentence_start/>Nonetheless, the present study is limited by sample size (see below), and meta-analyses combining multiple samples of directly-ascertained patients will indeed largely refine the gene list presented here and add other relevant genes, hopefully providing evidence convergent with results from registry-based studies.
Strengths and limitations

The main limitation of this study is its sample size, which is statistically small, though substantial when considering that PMS is a rare disorder, all patients were directly ascertained [<citation rid="CR46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s11689-024-09572-7" pmid="39363263" pmcid="PMC11451156" count="1">46</citation>], and the vast majority of similar studies published to date have a smaller sample size [<citation rid="CR3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/2040-2392-4-18" pmid="23758760" pmcid="PMC3707861" count="1">3</citation>, <citation rid="CR14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s11689-019-9273-1" pmcid="PMC6637483" pmid="31319798" count="1">14</citation>, <citation rid="CR35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13023-020-01592-5" pmid="33256793" pmcid="PMC7708101" count="1">35</citation>, <citation rid="CR42" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s11689-021-09370-5" pmid="34246244" pmcid="PMC8272382" count="1">42</citation>, <citation rid="CR44" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s11689-016-9150-0" pmid="27118998" pmcid="PMC4845478" count="1">44</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Instead, studies collecting data from registries can reach many more patients [<citation rid="CR40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13229-024-00619-z" pmid="39350236" pmcid="PMC11443936" count="1">40</citation>], at the expense of reliability and precision, as investigators have no control over information provided by family members and no direct interactions with the patient. <sentence_start/>In the latter setting, some clinical phenotypes cannot be explored, while others require caution because parents may overlook or overemphasize some behaviors/traits. <sentence_start/>In our opinion, direct ascertainment can yield the most reliable results and allow to explore a broader array of phenotypes. <sentence_start/>Nonetheless, we acknowledge the relatively large regions of association stemming from our limited statistical power (Table 3). <sentence_start/>Furthermore, some results are sufficiently clear-cut, but for other phenotypic features additional thresholds may have been missed. <sentence_start/>Ultimately, merging and meta-analyzing data from several direct-ascertainment studies may represent the best strategy to enhance statistical power while retaining maximum reliability.

Furthermore, most 22q deletions carried by our patients are simple rearrangements, but we cannot exclude phenotypic effects by at least two additional mechanisms which were not investigated here, namely (a) an abnormal epigenetic modulation of gene expression in the residual allele, and (b) complex chromosomal rearrangements and uniparental disomy yielding a global alteration of the three-dimensional chromatin architecture of chromosome 22, as previously described in a subset of patients with 22q deletions and PMS [<citation rid="CR149" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ejhg.2008.195" pmid="18854866" pmcid="PMC2682770" count="1">149</citation>, <citation rid="CR150" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/jmedgenet-2017-105125" pmid="29378768" pmcid="PMC5869459" count="1">150</citation>].
Conclusions

The present study, in conjunction with the recently published clinical phenotyping of our PMS sample [<citation rid="CR46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s11689-024-09572-7" pmid="39363263" pmcid="PMC11451156" count="1">46</citation>], provides new evidence supporting a significant correlation between terminal deletion size in chr 22q11.3 and several phenotypes including verbal language, motor development timing, gait, muscle strength, social cognition (i.e. eye contact, reciprocal object exchange gesture, and joint attention), infectious diseases coincident with the behavioral onset of PMS, brain structural abnormalities on MRI, renal and upper urinary tract anomalies, dysmorphisms, and comorbidity with bipolar disorder. <sentence_start/>We find several recurrent thresholds pointing at strong candidate genes possibly involved in one or in several phenotypes through their important role in neurodevelopment (<italic toggle="yes">BRD1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">TBC1D22A</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">ATXN10</italic> and/or <italic toggle="yes">FBLN1</italic>), and morphogenesis (<italic toggle="yes">PLXNB2, TAFA5</italic>). <sentence_start/>Only for renal malformations, the two maximum likelihood thresholds both point toward long non-coding RNAs and antisense RNAs, whose functional impact deserves further investigation. <sentence_start/>Larger samples will be able to refine these results and to detect additional phenotypic characteristics influenced by genes other than <italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic>. <sentence_start/>Other genes involved in very large deletions yield serious consequences on brain morphology, motor and cognitive function, a well-known example consisting in <italic toggle="yes">TCF20</italic> [<citation rid="CR134" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nn.4352" pmid="27479843" count="1">134</citation>-<citation rid="CR136" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ejhg.2016.90" pmid="27436265" pmcid="PMC5117939" count="1">136</citation>], located at 8,577 kb from the telomeric end (Table 2). <sentence_start/>Our results should not be interpreted as overlooking the role of these more centromeric genes, rather as demonstrating that smaller deletions can be equally disruptive because they already span genes closer to <italic toggle="yes">SHANK3,</italic> which play a critical role in multiple clinically-relevant phenotypes, including CNS structure and function. <sentence_start/>This line of investigation is important, because it can significantly improve the clinical management of PMS patients by conferring valuable prognostic information to clinicians on the basis of deletion size already at the time of genetic diagnosis. <sentence_start/>The replication and consistency among studies assessing different cohorts of clinically-characterized PMS patients carrying chr 22q13 terminal deletions, as well as interstitial deletions sparing <italic toggle="yes">SHANK3</italic>, will be instrumental in reliably mapping the precise landscape of genotype-phenotype correlations in Phelan-McDermid syndrome. <sentence_start/>Future investigations will also need to address additional mechanisms able to contribute to the heterogeneity of the clinical phenotype, in conjunction with deletion size.
